Yes, there's a lot. The profiling pass prototyped a set of fixes, and with all of them on the run time roughly halves while the output stays the same. I re-ran both checks myself:

| Corpus | Now | Fixes, current allocator | Fixes + mimalloc |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 82.3 ms | 41.4 ms | 34.7 ms (−58%) |
| spectrum | 63.1 ms | 48.5 ms | 45.2 ms (−28%) |

The output hashed the same as the current build on all five corpora, ignoring the `durationMs` field.

**Where the time goes now:** more than half of Mantine's run is not extraction. It is copying, freeing and single-threaded JSON writing of a 19 MB output. Inside the props-resolving step, half of the CPU goes to the macOS memory allocator contending across 18 threads.

**Ranked fixes, all with identical output:**

| # | Fix | Saving (mantine / spectrum) | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Use the mimalloc allocator in the CLI | −21 / −9 ms | Low; uses about 36 MB more memory |
| 2 | Skip freeing the whole result at CLI exit | −15 / −9 ms | Low |
| 3 | Move resolved components into the output instead of copying them (`revision.rs:382`) | −11 / −6 ms, partly overlaps #2 | Low |
| 4 | Write the JSON in parallel, per component, through a buffered stdout | −10 / −3 ms | Low |
| 5 | Resolve each inherited prop declaration once instead of per component; each Mantine style prop is resolved 236 times (`chain.rs:257`) | −7 ms / ~0 | Medium: the cache key must capture all resolver state |
| 6 | Build cycle-check keys by hashing instead of `format!("{:?}")` text (`named.rs:32`, `chain.rs:39`) | −4 / −1 ms | Low–medium |
| 7 | Cache import lookups and use integer file ids | about −2–4 ms (estimated) | Low |
| 8 | Start parsing while directory discovery is still running | −1.5 / −4 ms | Low |

**Fixed cost on every run:**
- **Directory walker:** it spends 2.9 ms of the 6.4 ms startup on 12 threads that wait in 1 ms sleep loops. Walking small trees on one thread saves about 2.5 ms.
- **Projects with TypeScript installed:** the parsed TypeScript declaration cache adds about 10 ms to every warm run (16.7 ms instead of 6.4). It decodes every entry and makes deep copies. The benchmark corpora don't exercise this because they have no `node_modules`, so real projects are slower than our numbers show. Loading it lazily and sharing instead of copying saves an estimated 5–7 ms.

**Other paths:**
- **`--format rdt`:** 33 ms slower than `--json` on Mantine, because it builds a JSON tree in memory and then pretty-prints it. Writing it directly would save an estimated 30 ms.
- **Watch mode:** an edit to a leaf component takes 21 ms, of which 18 ms is rebuilding the whole output. Sharing unchanged components instead of copying them should bring it to about 3–4 ms (estimated).

**A bug the profiling hit:** `--out /dev/null` fails with a permission error, because the atomic write creates its temp file in the target's directory (`/dev`). Any output path in a directory without write access fails the same way.

**Not worth doing:**
- **Parsing:** OXC takes 13 ms of CPU on Mantine; the parse time is mostly opening files.
- **Directory walking:** it is bound by the file system and already faster than `find`.
- **Curated HTML attributes:** they cost about 3 ms.
- **Removing repeated types from the JSON:** it would make Mantine's output about 45% smaller, but it changes the output format.

My proposal is three PRs against main:

1. Fixes 1–4 plus the `/dev/null` bug. Low risk, and most of the gain.
2. Fixes 5–6, with tests showing that sharing results across components doesn't change any component's props or warnings.
3. The startup fixes, the `--format rdt` writer and the watch-mode sharing, plus a benchmark project with TypeScript installed so the declaration cache is measured.

Should I start on PR 1?

The instrumented copy and the reproduction scripts are in `/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/perf/`.

Agreed: deduplicate, and do it before v1. Interning whole props beats interning only their types. The data stays the same; the file gets much smaller and much faster to parse:

| Corpus | Variant | Raw | gzip | Distinct / total | `JSON.parse` in Node |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | as today | 19.3 MB | 0.83 MB | 19,506 / 19,506 | 34.1 ms |
| mantine | types interned | 10.4 MB | 0.51 MB | 1,280 / 19,506 | 12.5 ms |
| mantine | **whole props interned** | **3.6 MB** | **0.19 MB** | 3,137 / 19,506 | **4.5 ms** |
| spectrum | as today | 6.9 MB | 0.29 MB | 6,685 / 6,685 | 10.0 ms |
| spectrum | **whole props interned** | **4.2 MB** | **0.22 MB** | 2,399 / 6,685 | **5.6 ms** |

Whole props win because inherited props have the same name, type, description and declaring type on every component. A prop whose default value differs on one component simply becomes its own table entry. The Vite plugin and NAPI consumers parse this JSON, so this saves them about 30 ms on Mantine on top of the Rust-side savings.

## Design points for deduplication

- **IDs must be content hashes, not array positions.** Positions shift between watch revisions; hash IDs stay the same across edits. A watch update then only sends new table entries and drops entries nothing uses any more.
- **Scope:** only the canonical output changes. `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` stay expanded because they exist for compatibility. The npm package gets an `expand()` helper and `index.d.ts` types for the table.
- **Rust side:** storing shared props once also removes most of the copy-and-free cost from fixes 2–3, and makes the 19 MB write about 5× smaller.
- **Contract change:** it changes the output schema, so it needs a schema version bump and an ADR. AGENTS.md requires an ADR for `PropType` serialization changes. The release is held, so this is the cheapest time to break the format.

## JSON crates

None of them is a big lever here. Measured on Mantine's 19.3 MB output, all byte-identical:

| | Write | Read into a JSON value |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| serde_json (current) | 12.5 ms | 54 ms |
| **sonic-rs** | **8.1 ms** | **7.6 ms** |
| simd-json | 10.8 ms | — |

- **sonic-rs** is a drop-in for our serde types. It saves 4.4 ms on Mantine today, but after deduplication the output is about 3.6 MB, so the saving drops to roughly 1 ms.
- **Reading JSON** is not on our hot path; we only read tsconfig and package.json, through oxc_resolver.
- I'd skip a new crate for now and revisit after deduplication.

The bigger JSON costs are in our own code, not the library:

1. **`CollectedType`** serializes and deserializes by building a `serde_json::Value` tree first (`crates/core/src/types/collected.rs:465-477`). That covers the msgpack declaration cache, so it's most of the 6.9 ms warm-cache decode. Deriving the serde impls directly (with a cache schema bump) should remove most of it.
2. **`--format rdt`** builds `json!` trees, with key order preserved, then pretty-prints them. That costs 33 ms more than `--json` on Mantine. Writing derived structs directly would save about 30 ms.

## Proposed order

1. **PR: low-risk speedups.** mimalloc, no free at exit, move instead of copy, parallel writing, and the `--out /dev/null` bug.
2. **ADR and PR: deduplicated canonical output.** Content-hash prop table, schema bump, `expand()` helper, and watch updates that carry only new table entries.
3. **PR: serialization.** Direct serde for `CollectedType` and a streamed `--format rdt` writer.
4. **Then:** resolution sharing (fixes 5–6) and the startup fixes.

content.text:
You're right, it doesn't need to. Only `--format rdt` has to stay expanded, because its whole point is to look exactly like RDT's output.

`--format storybook` is a JSON map from component key to a `__docgenInfo`-shaped object (`crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs:132`). Nothing in the repo reads it: the Vite plugin uses the canonical output, and there's no Storybook integration yet. Storybook never reads this file anyway. It reads `Component.__docgenInfo` at runtime, from whatever code injects it. So the injector decides the runtime shape, and it can work from a deduplicated file in either of two ways:

1. **Expand at injection time:** the injector looks up each component's props in the table and builds full objects.
2. **Emit JS with shared constants:** `const p0 = {…}; Button.__docgenInfo = { props: { c: p0, … } }`. The emitted code stays deduplicated, yet at runtime Storybook sees normal, fully populated objects. Memory drops too, because inherited props become one shared object.

The one risk with option 2: if Storybook ever mutates a prop object, the change would show up on every component sharing it. I believe its argTypes extraction builds new objects rather than mutating, but I haven't verified that; a test that freezes the objects would confirm it.

My recommendation: deduplicate both the canonical and storybook formats now, and keep only `rdt` expanded. When we build the Storybook docgen provider, it emits the shared-constant JS. Another option is to drop `--format storybook` entirely and have the provider work from the canonical output, since nothing uses the storybook format today.

Yes. Once the provider is our own package, `--format storybook` has no job left, and I'd drop it.

- **Use the binding, not the CLI.** The provider should read the canonical output through the NAPI watch session the Vite plugin already uses, not by running the CLI and parsing its stdout. The session gives incremental updates for HMR without a process per run, and `storybook build` can use the same path. `--json` stays useful for CI and other tools.
- **Canonical is the better input anyway.** It has:
  - structured types, so union members map straight to select controls instead of being parsed back out of strings
  - `detectedBy`
  - diagnostics, which tell the provider when to fall back to RCM for a component
  - (once it lands) the deduplicated prop table, so shared props become shared objects at runtime for free
- **The open question is where the canonical-to-Storybook mapping lives.** Today the PropType-to-RDT-type mapping (enum values, raw text) exists only in Rust, inside the CLI crate (`serialize_rdt` in `crates/cli/src/commands/extract.rs`). If the provider maps in JS, we have two copies that can drift. Either:

  2. make the JS provider the only Storybook mapping and keep Rust's copy for `--format rdt` alone.

  Which is right depends on what Storybook 11's provider API wants back: RDT-shaped `__docgenInfo`, or RCM's component-meta shape. That's the first thing to check from Storybook's source. If it's RDT-shaped, option 1; if it's RCM-shaped, the mapping is new and belongs in the provider.

Profiling showed half of a large project's extraction went to copying, freeing and serializing the output on one thread, and that the system allocator serialized the resolver's rayon workers. Output is byte-identical.

## Changes

- `extract()` moves each resolved entry and its diagnostics into the output instead of cloning them, and frees the rest of the revision on a background thread. Watch keeps the copying path, since later revisions need `resolved`.
- `extraction_output_to_json` (CLI `--json`, NAPI `extractAll`/`initializeSession`) serializes components in parallel and splices them in as raw JSON. A test asserts it matches `serde_json::to_string` byte for byte, and destructuring `ExtractionOutput` makes a new field a compile error.
- The CLI uses mimalloc, streams `--json` through a buffered stdout and skips freeing the output at exit.
- Fix: `--out` to a device or FIFO (`/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`) failed with EPERM because the atomic write put its temp file in `/dev`. With enough permission the rename would have replaced the device. Non-regular targets are now written in place.

## Measurements

Fastest of 40 runs, `extract --src DIR --json`, M5 Max, before = main:

| Corpus | Before | After | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 82.7 ms | 41.1 ms | −50% |
| chakra | 21.9 ms | 17.7 ms | −19% |
| antd | 35.9 ms | 23.7 ms | −34% |
| shadcn | 35.7 ms | 31.9 ms | −11% |
| spectrum | 63.2 ms | 47.4 ms | −25% |

`--json` output hashes are identical on all five corpora (`durationMs` normalized).

- `just test-rust`, `just lint doc-check machete typos`
- `pipeline::tests::parallel_json_writer_matches_serde_json_byte_for_byte`
- `output::tests::write_atomic_writes_a_device_in_place_instead_of_renaming_over_it`

content.text:
No. PR #94 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/94) is only the low-risk speedups, and its output is byte-identical to main. Deduplication changes the canonical output format, so it needs an ADR and a schema bump in its own PR. The Storybook research just came back and changes how to frame that, so here's your earlier question first.

## How Storybook gets docgen today

**Storybook 10.6.3 (latest stable): injected at build time.**
- **Default `typescript.reactDocgen: 'react-docgen'`:** a Vite plugin parses each file and appends `;Button.__docgenInfo={…}` for every component *defined* in that file. Barrels and re-exports get nothing.
- **`'react-docgen-typescript'`:** `@joshwooding/vite-plugin-react-docgen-typescript` builds a TypeScript program from your tsconfig, appends `Button.displayName = …; Button.__docgenInfo = {…}` inside a try/catch, and invalidates dependent modules on HMR.
- **`false`:** no docgen plugin runs.
- **Webpack** works the same way, through a loader and a plugin.

**At runtime,** `@storybook/react` reads `component.__docgenInfo.props` and converts it to argTypes:
- It picks the format from the **first prop only**: a `type` field means RDT, `tsType` means react-docgen.
- `type: {name: 'enum', value: [{value: '"a"'}]}` becomes a radio control (five options or fewer) or a select.
- Default values must be unquoted strings with no `computed` or `func` keys.
- `@ignore` in a prop's description drops that prop.
- Nothing mutates the prop objects, so shared objects are safe.

**Storybook 11 (`11.0.0-alpha.7`): docgen moves to the server.**
- `features.docgenServer` is on by default whenever `typescript` resolves. The builder plugins are then skipped and nothing is injected. Builder docgen is deprecated, and the deprecation message says it is removed in Storybook 12.
- Docgen comes from a chain of providers registered through `experimental_docgenProvider`. That hook already exists in 10.6.3, behind `features.experimentalDocgenServer`.
- Each provider runs in a Node worker thread. It receives the story index entry and returns a `DocgenPayload` with **already-converted argTypes**.
- React's default provider is react-component-meta (a TypeScript language service), and its props still use the RDT shape.
- Storybook re-asks a provider only about components it has already extracted whose stories changed; the provider must keep its own data fresh.

## What this means for us

- **Target the Storybook 11 provider.** It's where Storybook is going and it's server-side. Register ours last so it wraps React's provider; if Caliper answers without calling the next provider, the TypeScript language service is never even built. A Vite plugin that injects `__docgenInfo` (with `reactDocgen: false`) covers Storybook 10.
- **Storybook never sees our canonical JSON.** In both paths we convert to RDT-shaped props, or straight to argTypes, inside our own integration. So deduplication is internal to binding → provider, and it still pays: smaller strings across NAPI and less parsing.
- **`--format storybook` really is unnecessary;** neither path uses it.
- **Unknowns to settle in a spike:**
  - Does our NAPI binding load inside `worker_threads`?
  - React's props-to-argTypes conversion isn't a public export, so we'd reimplement it from `storybook/internal/docs-tools` or import the browser bundle.
  - The provider has to resolve the story's `meta.component` to the component file itself.
  - Everything is `experimental_` and alpha.

## Next steps

1. **Deduplication:** draft the ADR (content-hash prop table, schema bump, `expand()` helper, watch updates carrying only new entries), then the PR.
2. **Storybook spike:**
   - check that the NAPI binding works inside a worker thread
   - write a minimal `createDocgenProvider` that answers from a Caliper session for one Mantine story
   - convert props to argTypes and compare the result with react-component-meta's

Want me to start both?

result: PR #94 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/94) contains only the byte-identical speedups (Mantine 83 → 41 ms, Spectrum 63 → 47 ms), not deduplication. Storybook 10 injects `__docgenInfo` at build time, and Storybook 11 moves docgen to server-side providers that return argTypes, so Caliper should ship a Storybook 11 provider plus a Storybook 10 Vite plugin and deduplicate its own output separately.
I think we should start on the dedupe work right? Based on the storybook findings?

Partly. The Storybook findings don't argue for deduplication: Storybook never sees our canonical JSON, and Storybook 11 asks the provider one component at a time. The case for it stands on its own, though. I'm checking one claim before committing to it: whether the Vite plugin ships the whole output to the browser.

# 0009. Write each distinct prop once in the canonical output

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-21

## Context

Inherited props repeat on every component that inherits them. On Mantine, 19,506 props hold 3,137 distinct values, and the canonical JSON is 19.3 MB. The Vite plugin serves that whole output as its virtual module and re-serves it after every edit, so the browser downloads and parses all of it (34 ms in `JSON.parse` on Mantine) each time. Storybook does not read this format: both its build-time `__docgenInfo` and its Storybook 11 docgen providers take RDT-shaped props, which an integration converts to.

## Decision

The canonical JSON (CLI `--json` and `--format canonical`, NAPI `extractAll` and `initializeSession`, watch updates) writes each distinct prop once, in a top-level `props` table, and components refer to it by id.

- `components[key].props` and `components[key].notableInherited` map a prop name to an id; `props[id]` is the full prop.
- An id is the 64-bit FNV-1a hash of the prop's compact JSON, as 16 hex digits. The same prop gets the same id in every output and update a build writes, so a client can merge tables. Two different props with one id fail serialization instead of one silently replacing the other.
- An `IncrementalUpdate` carries `props` with every entry its `updatedComponents` reference. A client merges it into its table and may drop ids no component references any more.
- Interning is a wire-format concern only. The Rust types keep each `ComponentEntry`'s props inline, and `ComponentEntry` on its own still serializes them inline.
- `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` stay inline: they exist to match other tools' shapes.

## Consequences

- Mantine's output drops from 19.3 MB to 3.6 MB and its parse from 34 ms to 4.5 ms; Spectrum's from 6.9 MB to 4.2 MB.
- Breaking for every reader of the canonical format: a prop is now one lookup away. `packages/napi/index.d.ts` types the table, and readers that want inline props expand them.
- Ids are opaque. They change when a prop's serialized form changes, including across versions, so nothing may store one beyond the output it came from.
- A hash collision fails the whole write. At 100,000 distinct props the chance is about 3 in 10 billion.

## Alternatives considered

- **Positional ids** (index into a table array): shorter, but the same prop moves between revisions, so every watch update would have to resend the table.
- **Interning only types**: the type is half of a repeated prop; descriptions, parents and tags repeat too. Mantine stays at 10.4 MB.
- **Compression only**: gzip already shrinks the output to 0.83 MB in transit, but the reader still parses 19.3 MB.

input.new_string:
The Rust types hold props inline, but the canonical JSON does not (ADR 0009, `types/output/interned.rs`). `ExtractionOutput` serializes each distinct `ParsedProp` once, in a top-level `props` table keyed by id, and each component's `props` and `notableInherited` map a prop name to an id. An id is the FNV-1a 64 hash of the prop's compact JSON as 16 hex digits, so identical props share one entry and keep their id across watch revisions. `IncrementalUpdate` writes its `updatedComponents` the same way, with a `props` table holding every prop they refer to. A `ComponentEntry` serialized on its own (snapshot tests, `ExtractionOutput`'s `Deserialize` after expanding ids) still holds its props inline.

**Invariant 6a:** two different props never share an id. `PropTable::add` compares the JSON of every prop added under an existing id and fails serialization on a mismatch, rather than letting one prop stand in for another.

Stacked on #94.

Inherited props repeat on every component that inherits them: Mantine's canonical output was 19.3 MB for 3,137 distinct props. The Vite plugin's virtual module is `export default <whole output>` and is re-served after every edit, so the browser downloaded and parsed all of it each time. Decision and trade-offs: `docs/adr/0009-canonical-output-interns-props.md`.

## Format

- Top-level `props: { [id]: ParsedProp }`; a component's `props` and `notableInherited` map prop name → id.
- id = FNV-1a 64 of the prop's compact JSON, 16 hex digits: the same prop has the same id in every output and update of a build. Two different props with one id fail serialization (compared by JSON bytes, not `PartialEq`, so `NaN` literals compare correctly).
- `IncrementalUpdate` (and the Vite plugin's `caliper-docgen:update`) carries `props` with every prop its `updatedComponents` refer to.
- Covers `extract --json`, `--format canonical`, NAPI `extractAll`/`initializeSession`, watch `--out`. `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` keep props inline.
- Interning is serialization-only: the Rust types and `ComponentEntry`'s own serde keep props inline. `ExtractionOutput`'s `Deserialize` expands ids.

## Measurements

`extract --src DIR --json`, fastest of 30 runs, before = main:

| Corpus | Time before | Time after | Size before | Size after | Node `JSON.parse` before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 81.8 ms | 44.0 ms | 19.3 MB | 3.6 MB | 41.3 ms | 6.0 ms |
| chakra | 21.2 ms | 18.6 ms | 0.8 MB | 0.6 MB | 1.2 ms | 0.9 ms |
| antd | 34.3 ms | 25.4 ms | 2.0 MB | 1.6 MB | 3.6 ms | 3.1 ms |
| shadcn | 36.9 ms | 32.6 ms | 3.9 MB | 2.5 MB | 6.0 ms | 3.3 ms |
| spectrum | 61.8 ms | 48.4 ms | 6.9 MB | 4.3 MB | 12.4 ms | 7.3 ms |

Time includes #94. On top of #94 alone, Mantine costs about 3 ms more, because every prop is serialized once to compute its id.

## Verify

- Fixture snapshots are unchanged (they render props inline), and `snapshots.rs` asserts every fixture's canonical JSON reads back into the same output.
- `types::output::interned::tests`: FNV-1a test vectors, sharing and distinct defaults, expanded ids equal `ComponentEntry`'s own JSON, round trip, missing id, collision.
- `pipeline::watch::tests::an_updates_props_are_exactly_the_ones_its_components_refer_to_and_applying_it_matches_the_session`
- `just test-rust`, `just test-ts`, `just test-integration`, `just lint doc-check machete typos`

GitHub's status for one job, "Changesets", got stuck: every step finished, but the job never reported done, so the PR showed it as pending for hours. I re-ran that one job and it passed in 49 seconds. None of my workflow changes were involved; that job dates from 2026-09-26 (`9fb77d85`). Separately, my local test runs were slow because the machine was loaded by other jobs and I piped the suite into `head`. The full Rust suite takes 4.5 seconds.

**Deduplication is up as #95** (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/95), stacked on #94 because both change the same serialization code. All its checks pass in about 2 minutes, and so do #94's.

- **Format:** the output now has a top-level `props` table. Each component's `props` and `notableInherited` map a prop name to an id: a 16-hex hash of the prop's JSON, so the same prop has the same id across runs and watch updates. If two different props ever hashed to the same id, the write fails instead of mixing them up.
- **Watch updates** carry only the props their changed components use. A test applies an update the way a client would and checks it ends up identical to the session.
- **What changes:** `--json`, `--format canonical`, the NAPI functions and the Vite plugin's virtual module. `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` stay expanded. The Rust types are unchanged.
- **The extracted data is the same:** all eight fixture snapshots are unchanged, and each fixture's new JSON reads back to the same output.
- **Also updated:** ADR 0009, the JSON schema, the NAPI typings, the Vite plugin payload and README, `apps/validate`, the architecture docs, and a changeset marking it a breaking minor release.

| Corpus | RDT | Caliper | Speed | RDT memory | Caliper memory | Memory |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 1,195 ms | 42 ms | 29× | 473 MB | 126 MB | 3.8× |
| chakra | 570 ms | 18 ms | 31× | 315 MB | 41 MB | 7.6× |
| antd | 811 ms | 26 ms | 31× | 411 MB | 53 MB | 7.8× |
| shadcn | 1,270 ms | 34 ms | 38× | 620 MB | 60 MB | 10.3× |
| spectrum | 1,223 ms | 49 ms | 25× | 539 MB | 85 MB | 6.3× |

- **Speed:** 30.7× on average, up from about 23× on current main. Mantine, the worst case, went from 15× to 29×.
- **Memory:** 7.2× less on average, about the same as on main. mimalloc uses a bit more memory, which offsets the savings from freeing less; Mantine's own ratio improved from 3.2× to 3.8×.
- **Both times are full process runs.** Node itself starts in 41 ms; the rest of RDT's time is loading TypeScript and parsing.
- **These corpora have no `node_modules`.** RDT can't resolve dependencies here, so it does less work than in a real project. A comparison with dependencies installed is still to be run, and both tools would be slower there.

Checked against the code. The agent's main claims hold.

## Benchmark with dependencies installed

| Project | RDT | Caliper, cold cache | Caliper, warm cache | Speed (cold) | Memory (cold) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 1,463 ms | 70 ms | 54 ms | 21× | 3.5× |
| chakra | 16,601 ms | 38 ms | 30 ms | 440× | 21× |
| shadcn | 3,166 ms | 53 ms | 45 ms | 59× | 13× |
| antd | 1,833 ms | 45 ms | 35 ms | 41× | 12× |
| spectrum | 2,537 ms | 94 ms | 84 ms | 27× | 3.3× |

On a cold cache that's a geometric mean of 57× faster and 8× less memory. Don't use those numbers: the two tools no longer do the same work.

- **RDT's output changed a lot.** Chakra went from 2.3k props to 745k once its style-prop types resolved.
- **Caliper's output didn't change on four of the five projects.** It now finds every package's module, except shadcn's 205 alias imports, but it never reads the types inside them.

## Why Caliper doesn't read `node_modules` types

- **Nothing ever loads a dependency's type definitions.** The pipeline parses only the project's own files, `@types/react` (in full mode) and TypeScript's lib files (`crates/core/src/pipeline/revision.rs:199-226`). When a component's prop type comes from a package, import resolution finds that package's `.d.ts` file but never parses it. The type stays an unexpanded name, with a "Cannot resolve type X (resolved to X in <pkg>.d.ts)" diagnostic.
  - `docs/STATUS.md` says "cross-package `.d.ts` resolution" is fully implemented; that only means finding the path.
  - The `.d.ts` parse cache exists for dependency types (`ARCHITECTURE.md` says so), but only lib and React files ever go through it.
- **tsconfig isn't auto-detected.** Main reads `paths` only from an explicitly configured `tsconfigPath`. #93 adds `extends` and wildcard support, but still only for a configured file. Neither reads `customConditions`, which chakra and spectrum use.

## Storybook doesn't avoid `node_modules`

Both of Storybook's engines use the TypeScript checker, which resolves every reachable type in `node_modules`: RDT (optional in Storybook 10) and react-component-meta (the default in Storybook 11). What Storybook filters is which props it *shows*:

- **RDT's default filter** hides a prop when the type that declares it lives in `node_modules`.
- **react-component-meta**:
  - hides React's own `Attributes` and `RefAttributes`
  - hides a package's props only when more than 30 come from the same source
  - honours `@ignore`

So with default settings, Storybook still shows two things Caliper gets wrong:

1. **Project props whose types come from a package, fully resolved.** Examples: chakra's `size` as `ConditionalValue<"sm" | "md" | …>`, which becomes a select control, and antd's `closable` as `boolean | ClosableType`. Caliper shows the bare type name instead, so there's no select control.
2. **Small sets of props declared in a package, under react-component-meta.** For example, Radix's `side`, `align` and `asChild` on shadcn components. Caliper gives those components no props at all.

## Recommendation

1. **Load the dependency types that project imports reach.** Before resolving components, resolve each import to its `.d.ts`, parse it through the existing cache in parallel, and follow its own imports and re-exports until nothing new turns up. Resolving stays a pure, parallel step, and watch mode can track these files as dependencies.
2. **Find the tsconfig automatically.** `oxc_resolver` can discover the nearest tsconfig for each file; we'd also pass its `customConditions` to the resolver.
3. **Match Storybook's display rules for package-declared props.** Use react-component-meta's rules (hide React's attributes, hide sources with more than 30 props), so output doesn't balloon the way RDT's chakra run did.

This changes pipeline structure and output, so it needs an ADR, and the speed comparison must be re-measured afterwards. It's the biggest precision gap the Storybook use case exposes. Should I start with the ADR?

The benchmark scripts are in `/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/bench-deps/`, in run order `install.sh` → `prune.sh` → `restore-files.py` → `resolve-check.sh` → `bench.sh` → `report.py`.

Storybook doesn't skip `node_modules`; it only hides some package-declared props. Next step is an ADR to load dependency types that project imports reach.

content.text:
Partly. RDT's exclusions shrink its output, but they don't make it do less type work. I checked RDT 2.4.0's source:

- **`propFilter`** (including `{ skipPropsWithoutDoc, skipPropsWithName }`, and Storybook's default node_modules filter) runs *after* the work. `getPropsInfo` resolves every prop and renders its type text first; the filter only deletes entries from the result (`react-docgen-typescript/lib/parser.js:262-269`). Chakra's 745k props were all computed whether or not they were filtered.
- **Storybook's `include`/`exclude` globs** choose which project files get documented. The TypeScript program still loads the full import closure of those files.
- **Only compiler options load less:** `"types": []` (no automatic `@types` packages), `paths` mapping a package to a stub, or `noResolve`. `skipLibCheck` skips *checking* `.d.ts` files, not reading them.

For our design, the takeaway is that RDT has no "don't load what you won't show" lever; its filters are display filters. If we load dependency types, we can do better: load only the declarations that the props we emit reference, and apply Storybook's display filter before rendering type text rather than after.

The two analysis passes are still running: the code paths a dependency type would flow through, and the measured size and parse cost of each project's dependency closure. The full structural answer (architecture, semantic models, performance) comes once both are back.

Pipeline phases and data flow **Current behavior** - Everything runs in `Revision::resolve_cold`, crates/core/src/pipeline/revision.rs:159-267. - Discover: `discover_files(&options.src_dirs, …)` at :166. - Parse in parallel with rayon at :171-185, through `parse_source_file` (:517-533). Only `.d.ts` files go through `DtsCache`. - Merge sequentially with `global.merge(&path, data)` at :187-197. - Phase 3.5: in Full mode only, `@types/react` is resolved and merged (:202-218). - Phase 3.6: `lib.es5.d.ts` and `lib.dom.d.ts` are merged in every mode (:221-227). Both use `merge_cached_dts_file`, called one file at a time, not in parallel. - Then `Arc::new(global)` (:229), `NamedTypeIndex::build` (:230), `compute_ambient_global_files` (:231), `ResolutionContext::new_with_cached_ambient_global_files` (:232-237), `resolve_all` (:238) and `assemble` (:399-465). - **Which files get parsed** is decided in exactly three places: - `discover_files` (discover.rs). `excluded()` at discover.rs:105-115 drops anything under `node_modules` unless the source directory itself is inside one. - The react merge (revision.rs:204). - The lib merge (revision.rs:222). - `merge_cached_dts_file` (pipeline/mod.rs:202-230) does three things: - Drains the file's diagnostics into `lib_diagnostics` (:224). That includes Info `SkippedCandidate` diagnostics, because component detection runs on `.d.ts` files. - Clears component mappings: `data.component_mappings.clear()` (:228). - Merges the result into `global`. - **Immutable during resolve: yes.** - `ResolutionContext` is documented as "Shared, read-only" (resolver/mod.rs:195-232) and holds `global: Arc`, `import_map`, `named_types`, `oxc_resolver`, `enum_bare_index` and `const_array_bare_index`, all built once in `build` (:253-300). - The only state that changes during resolve is the `module_resolutions` DashMap memo (:209-210) and the thread-local dependency recorder (deps.rs:26-28). - **Nothing can add files during resolve.** `resolve_import_specifier` returns a path and never parses it. - Watch: `Revision::next` (revision.rs:271-394) clones the whole `GlobalSourceData` and `NamedTypeIndex` on every edit (`(*self.global).clone()` at :277-278). - It runs `remove_file` and `merge_file`, then rebuilds a fresh `ResolutionContext` (:323-328). - That rebuild includes `ImportResolutionMap::build` over all of `global` (resolver/mod.rs:289) and the enum bare-name indexes. - `GlobalSourceData::remove_file` (types/global.rs:137-148) is a prefix scan with `retain` over every key. **Implications** - Dependency loading has to happen before line 229, in one of two ways: - Eagerly: walk the import graph from project imports, resolve specifiers, parse transitively, then merge. This needs its own parallel parse, because the current merge path is serial. - Lazily: resolve would need interior mutability (an on-demand parse cache behind a lock). That breaks the "built once, then read" design and the determinism of `resolve_all`. - The eager path is a fixpoint over imports and re-exports (`export *`, `export {} from`), which needs specifier resolution before a `ResolutionContext` exists. `resolve_package_dts_path` (resolver/mod.rs:320-329) is the existing precedent for that. - Performance: every watch edit currently costs O(all merged data) for the clones (:277-278), the `remove_file` retain scans, `ImportResolutionMap::build` and the enum indexes. - Adding dependency data multiplies that per-edit cost; lib.dom is already the largest file in it. - A split is strongly indicated: an immutable `Arc` dependency/lib layer that `next()` shares, plus a mutable project layer. ## 2. Import and type resolution **`resolve_to_canonical`** (resolver/import.rs:38-66) - It first calls `find_import(file, name)`. On a hit it resolves the specifier, then runs `follow_reexports(resolved_file, exported_name)`. - Otherwise it splits `A.B` at the first `.`. If `A` is a namespace import (`exported_name == "*"`, :60), it follows `B` from the namespace's module (:58-65). - It returns `None` for a local name. Callers then fall back to `(consuming_file, name)` (precedence.rs:47-48). **`resolve_import_specifier`** (import.rs:203-239) and **`ModuleResolution`** (:192-200) - The memo is keyed `(dir, specifier)` (:211-219). `resolve_module` (:241-266) handles bare specifiers with `react::resolve_package_types_file` (react.rs:129-142). - That function tries `resolve_dts` and accepts `.d.ts`, `.d.mts` or `.d.cts`, then retries `@types/`. A hit becomes `ModuleResolution::PackageTypes(path)`. - Relative paths go through `oxc_resolver.resolve` and become `File(path)`. - `PackageTypes(path) => Some(path)` (:221) records **no** dependency. `File` calls `deps::record(&path)` (:222-225). `Unresolved` pushes a Warning `UnresolvableImport` "Cannot resolve '{spec}' from '{file}'" (:226-237). **`follow_reexports`** (:75-123) - It records `file`, then stops if `named_types.is_declared_at(file, name)` is true (types only, meaning interface or alias). Otherwise it uses `resolve_reexport_chain` (import_map.rs:94-122): - `Named` hops. - `Wildcards` tries each `export *` target and keeps the first one where the name is declared. - `ReExportNamespace` (`export * as Ns`) is ignored (import_map.rs:112). - Depth is capped by `MAX_REEXPORT_DEPTH = 8`, and a visited set prevents loops. **What happens when the resolved file is a `node_modules` `.d.ts` that was never parsed** 1. `resolve_import_specifier` returns `Some(pkg.d.ts)`, with no diagnostic and no dependency recorded. 2. `follow_reexports` finds no declaration and no re-exports, so it returns `(pkg.d.ts, name)`. 3. `lookup_type_alias` and `lookup_interface` miss (precedence.rs:50-60), then `resolve_known` runs (:62). 4. In `named.rs` (type level), the remaining checks run in order: - React builtin fallback (:137-140). - The silent `Named` list (:146-174). - In-scope type parameters (:177). - The ambient lib lookup by bare name (:188-196). It does **not** check the binding, so an imported name that collides with a lib.dom global is silently taken as that global. - Finally a Warning `UnresolvableImport`: "Cannot resolve type 'X' in 'file' (resolved to 'X' in '.d.ts') — it will appear as an unexpanded named reference" (:199-214). 5. In `chain.rs` (props level), the checks are: - Step 2.5 React builtin (:150-156). - The `html_element_for` terminal (:160-162). - Step 6 Warning "Cannot resolve type …" plus the type name in `composes` (:168-181). 6. The " (resolved to …)" suffix comes from `unresolved_location_note` (resolver/mod.rs:75-87). **How the specific forms are handled for project files** - `export *` and `export { X } from` work through `follow_reexports`. Tests: pipeline/tests.rs:919, 968, 1001, 1064, 1460, 1558. - `export type { A } from` is recorded with `is_type_only` (extractor/visit.rs:77-90). - An import followed by `export { A }` is promoted to a re-export (extractor/mod.rs:299-315). - Namespace imports such as `RadixPrimitive.SelectProps` work (import.rs:58-65). Test: tests.rs:766, against the real `react.d.ts`. - `typeof X` → `resolve_typeof` (func.rs:83-113) only consults `enum_bare_index` (for cva). Otherwise it returns Info "could not statically evaluate" plus `Named`. - `ComponentProps`: - In an `extends` position, `extends.rs:79-82` → `component_props_of` (:120-158). That resolves `X` canonically, then searches **`ctx.global.component_mappings`** for `(canonical_file, canonical_name)`. - As a direct props type, `known::component_props` returns `Alias{"Pkg.Root"}` (known.rs:283-288). That leads to `resolve_props_chain("Pkg.Root")`, an interface/alias lookup that cannot match a value. **Would the same code work if the dependency's `SourceData` were present?** - **Types:** mostly yes, unchanged: - Lookups are keyed by canonical file. - Aliases carry their `file_path` (`alias.rs:31-97` resolves members against the alias's own file). - Interface members resolve against `iface.file_path` (chain.rs:261-263). - `AtFile` switches context (collected.rs:86). - `PackageTypes` would also need to call `deps::record` (see section 6). - **Values, which is what `ComponentProps` needs:** no. - `merge_cached_dts_file` clears `component_mappings` (mod.rs:228), so `component_props_of` cannot find `Root`. - `follow_reexports` and `is_declared_at` only know types, so a value re-exported through `export *` stops at the barrel. - What is needed: a non-emitted index of dependency value declarations (component mappings or declared consts), plus value-aware re-export following. - `export * as Ns from` and `import { Ns }` followed by `Ns.X` do not resolve: `exported_name != "*"` returns `None` at import.rs:60, and `ReExportNamespace` is ignored. ## 3. Extractor on `.d.ts` **Component detection does run on `.d.ts`:** `is_tsx = source_type.is_jsx() || source_type.is_typescript_definition()` (extractor/mod.rs:144-145). - The comment in `test_radix_button_dts` (extractor/tests.rs:250, "component detection is off") is stale. - Project `.d.ts` files in `src` are emitted as components on purpose: docs/benchmarks.md:177 counts 8 declaration-only fixtures. Tests: tests.rs:993-1001 `declare function`, :1376-1388 plain `.ts`, :1395-1420 matrix, :1720-1734. - Dependency declarations are kept out of the output only by `component_mappings.clear()` (pipeline/mod.rs:225-228). - Tests for that: - `full_mode_does_not_emit_components_declared_in_merged_react_types` (pipeline/tests.rs:466-482). - `initialize_in_full_mode_does_not_emit_components_declared_in_merged_react_types` (pipeline/watch/tests.rs:19-43). It asserts the names are exactly `["Button"]`; the ghost was `PureComponent`. - So the distinction has to be "dependency file vs project file", not ".d.ts vs .tsx". **Support by form** - `export declare const X: React.ForwardRefExoticComponent

>`: yes, as a component mapping via Pattern 5 (visit.rs:260-280, test tests.rs:1726). The variable itself is not stored as a value anywhere else. - `declare function`: yes, via `TSDeclareFunction` (visit.rs:290-291), with skip diagnostics suppressed for it (:300-308). Overloads produce one mapping per signature; the ordinal is assigned in revision.rs:105-115. - `declare namespace N` (and `namespace`): keys are qualified as `N.X` (visit.rs:180-186, scoped_key at extractor/mod.rs:260-266; test tests.rs:719-732). Only `React.` gets a bare-name fallback lookup (named_type_index.rs:32-33, 121-123, 149-173). - `declare module 'x' { … }` and `declare global { … }`: walked, but nothing is qualified. Contents are keyed under the declaring file (tests.rs:723-730 expects `file:Ambient`, `file:Global`), so an augmentation is **not** attached to the target module. - `export =` and `export as namespace`: no visitor, so nothing is recorded. - `export default`: `visit_export_default_declaration` (visit.rs:387-420) only detects components and records no `LexedExport` for `default`, so `import X from 'pkg'` of a type cannot follow it. - `export * from` and `export type { A } from`: yes (visit.rs:77-117). - `import("pkg").Type`: falls through to `CollectedType::Raw` (extractor/mod.rs:577-583). The resolver then makes it Opaque `UnsupportedExpression` with an Info diagnostic (collected.rs:141-150). - Generic defaults: dropped, because only parameter names are kept (visit.rs:150-155, 172-176). With fewer arguments, `build_substitution` (resolver/substitute.rs:40-70) warns `GenericArgumentMismatch` and leaves the parameters as placeholders. - Class declarations: only component detection through the `Component`/`PureComponent` heritage (visit.rs:351-385). Members are not collected as an interface. **Proven by real `.d.ts` parsing today** (pipeline/tests.rs) - Real `react.d.ts`: :485 (Full HTML attrs), :555 (SVG attrs), :711 (type-only import), :766 (namespace member). - Real lib files: :819 and :873. - Diagnostics drain: :17. ## 4. Keys, identity and globals - `GlobalSourceData` maps are keyed `"{abs_path}:{name}"` (types/global.rs:77-98). Merging the same key merges declarations (props and extends concatenated, :113-125). Nothing merges across files, so augmentations do not merge. - `NamedTypeIndex` (named_type_index.rs:27-34) is `PathKey → name → value`. Loading dependency types fits the architecture, provided three things change: types are loaded **before** resolution and **only for names the project actually references**; they live in a **separate, shared layer**; and the hand-written shortcuts are **ranked by where a type is declared rather than by its name**. Per-file parse cost is fine. Loading whole files is not, and our `.d.ts` cache makes things slower. ## The three problems underneath 1. **A project prop's type comes from a package.** For example antd's `closable: ClosableType`, chakra's `ConditionalValue<…>`, or react-number-format's `OnValueChange`. This needs the package's type declarations. 2. **Props come from a package component's value.** For example `ComponentProps`, or a shadcn component wrapping a Radix one. This needs the package's component declarations, and nothing indexes values today. 3. **Which package-declared props to show.** This is a display rule, separate from loading. Storybook resolves everything and then filters what it shows. ## How it fits the architecture | Concern | Today | Change | | --- | --- | --- | | When types load | Project files, `@types/react` and TypeScript lib files are merged before an immutable `ResolutionContext` is built; resolving is pure and parallel. | Load dependency declarations in that same pre-resolve phase, so resolving stays read-only and deterministic. Loading on demand during resolution would mean locks and order-dependent results, so no. | | What loads | Nothing from packages. | Follow names, not files. Start from the imported names the project uses in type positions (prop types, `extends`, type arguments, `typeof X`). Follow re-exports by name to the declaring file, parse it, then follow the names that declaration references, in parallel waves until nothing new turns up. | | Where it's stored | One flat `GlobalSourceData`, copied on every watch edit (`revision.rs:277`). | A separate dependency layer behind an `Arc`, shared by every revision, consulted after the project layer. Keys are file paths, so the layers never collide. Watch edits stop paying for dependency data. | | Shortcut precedence | Real declaration, then name-based shortcut (`VariantProps`, `SxProps`, `RenderProps`, `HTMLChakraProps`…). | **Project declaration → shortcut keyed by declaring package (`VariantProps` from `class-variance-authority`) → dependency declaration → builtin.** Without this, the real declarations would win and turn these into unresolved conditional types. Keying shortcuts by package is also task #7 (structural rules instead of names). | | Leaks into output | Dependency `.d.ts` only stays out of the output because `merge_cached_dts_file` clears its components. | Each file has an origin: project, dependency or lib. Dependency components go into a value index for `typeof`, never into the output. Dependency enums never become public enums or shadow project ones; today the bare-name enum index takes the first match in path order, and `node_modules` sorts first. | | Module resolution | tsconfig only when configured; conditions hard-coded; `.d.mts`/`.d.cts` not discovered or cached. | Find each file's tsconfig automatically (`oxc_resolver` supports this), honour `customConditions` and `typesVersions`, accept `.d.mts`/`.d.cts`, and use one resolver configuration for both loading and resolving. | | Watch mode | Dependency files are never watched; changing `node_modules` needs `rebuild()`. | Keep that. But when an edit introduces a new imported name, `next()` must load it into a new version of the shared layer; otherwise watch output stops matching a cold run (invariant 5). Loaded extra declarations can't change other lookups, because lookups are keyed by file. | ## Semantic model changes - **`SourceData` (extractor):** support package-typing forms that are missing today: - `export =` - `export * as Ns` and `import { Ns }` followed by `Ns.X` - `export default` of types - generic defaults (dropped today, which causes `GenericArgumentMismatch`) - `import("pkg").T` (`Raw` today) - namespace merging beyond React - a value-declaration index (`declare const X: ForwardRefExoticComponent

`) `declare module 'x'` augmentations can wait. Each of these needs a cache schema bump (ADR 0003). - **Origin:** every declaration carries project, dependency (with package name) or lib. `PropParent` and `InheritedLayer` gain the package, so display rules and Storybook's filter don't depend on a `node_modules` path substring. - **Output: where package-declared props go.** RDT puts them in `props`, and Storybook's RDT filter then hides them. react-component-meta shows them unless one source contributes more than 30. I'd follow react-component-meta: show small sets like Radix's `side`/`align`/`asChild` in `props`, and fold large ones into an `InheritedLayer` plus curated notable props, as HTML attributes work today. This is a display decision and needs its own ADR. - **Diagnostics:** - a package that ships no types - a declaration not loaded because of the budget below - "resolved through package X". This replaces today's "Cannot resolve (resolved to X in pkg.d.ts)". - **Semantic backend (ADRs 0006/0007):** no conflict. The structural pass handles declared types, interfaces, aliases and generic substitution across packages. The TypeScript backend keeps what needs a checker: conditional and mapped types, and inference. Fewer components get handed to it, and both report the same parent files. ## Performance, measured | Project | Checker loads (upper bound) | Files following imports, tooling roots excluded | Caliper parse, no cache | Today's whole run | | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | mantine | 674 files, 7.7 MB | 236 files, 1.7 MB | 14 ms | 54–70 ms | | chakra | 1,709 files, 8.4 MB | 1,462 files, 2.5 MB (mostly 1-line re-export stubs) | 40 ms | 30–38 ms | | antd | 1,513 files, 12.7 MB | 564 files, 1.6 MB | 21 ms | 35–45 ms | | spectrum | 527 files, 15.8 MB | 150 files, 1.2 MB | 14 ms | 84–94 ms | | shadcn | 6,306 files, 37.6 MB | 5,965 files, 34 MB | 135 ms | 45–53 ms | The parse times are upper bounds: the copied files couldn't resolve each other, so no type merging happened. Following names would load less than following whole files. - **Following files is the wrong unit.** shadcn's `registry/icons/__phosphor__.ts` re-exports 159 icons, which drags in 3,034 files; following names needs about 320. Package-declared props: follow react-component-meta's rule (show unless more than 30 come from one source), or RDT's (always put them in `props`)? 2. Does this all account for dev/watch mode?

Partly. The shared dependency layer covers watch-mode cost, but five dev-mode issues weren't addressed, and two of them change the design.

## Already covered

- **Per-edit cost:** dependency declarations live in an `Arc` layer that every revision shares, so an edit no longer copies them. Today `Revision::next` copies all type data on every save; that's part of the measured 21 ms per edit on a Mantine leaf component.
- **Dependencies are fixed for a session:** components that use a package type never need re-resolving for a project edit. Local declarations still win over package ones, and the existing watch dependency tracking already handles project files.

## Missing, and what to do

1. **Watch output must equal a cold run's.** Loading by name means an edit can add a reference to a package type the session never loaded.
   - `next()` must load it before resolving: a small wave, a few milliseconds, at most around 15 ms for a 2 MB file.
   - Removing a reference leaves extra declarations loaded. That's harmless for lookups, which are keyed by file, but **not for diagnostics**: a parse diagnostic from a package file a cold run would never load would differ.
   - So diagnostics about package files must attach to the reference that reached them, not to the loaded file. The same goes for the budget diagnostic.
   - The watch-equals-cold test needs four new cases: adding an import, removing it, shadowing a package name with a local declaration, and crossing the budget.
2. **Rebuilding resolver indexes per edit.** Today each edit rebuilds the import map and the enum indexes over *all* loaded data (`resolver/mod.rs:289`). Those indexes must be layered too: build the dependency part once and reuse it, rebuild only the project part. Otherwise package data puts back the cost the shared layer removed.
3. **Installing a package while the dev server runs.** Today `node_modules`, `package.json` and tsconfig changes are ignored until a manual `rebuild()` (`docs/architecture/pipeline-orchestration.md:113`). That's the dev-mode case most likely to show stale types (`pnpm add`, upgrades, a tsconfig edit).
   - Don't watch `node_modules`. Watch the lockfile, the `package.json` files and the discovered tsconfigs, and rebuild when any changes: a fresh dependency layer plus re-resolving every component, about one cold run (40–90 ms).
   - The Vite plugin can register these with `addWatchFile`. The CLI watcher adds them to its watch set.
4. **Storybook 11's provider has no Vite hooks.** It runs in a separate worker that Storybook calls per story, and Storybook only re-asks about stories whose files changed.
   - So the session needs an "ensure fresh" check per request: a cheap stat of the files it read plus the lockfile and tsconfigs, then apply what changed. react-component-meta does the same.
   - This is a session API addition, so design it in the groundwork phase, not after.
5. **Memory in long sessions.** The layer only grows with what gets referenced, and the budget caps it. A rebuild (point 3) resets it. No other cleanup is needed.

## Unaffected

- **Startup:** loading dependencies without the cache adds about 10–40 ms to the first extraction; edits after that don't pay it again.
- **HMR payload:** package-derived props arrive as ordinary `props` table entries in updates (#95's format), so nothing changes there.
- **Concurrency:** loading happens under the session's existing writer lock, and readers keep using the published revision.

Revised groundwork phase: tsconfig auto-discovery and conditions, origin tagging, the shared layer *with layered indexes*, lockfile/tsconfig-triggered rebuilds, and the "ensure fresh" session API. The watch-equals-cold cases go into the loader phase as acceptance tests.

result: Not fully. All of these go into the groundwork phase or the loader's acceptance tests.

content.text:
Yes. The measurements point at a sharper design: **bytes are cheap and files are expensive.** Caliper parsed lucide's 2 MB bundle in 4.7 ms (418 MB/s) and csstype's 0.9 MB in 5.3 ms. But the import closures cost about 25 µs per file, mostly opening and reading it; chakra's 1,462 small files took 40 ms. So the clever design touches as few files as possible, and uses parallelism to hide the rest behind work we already do.

## The levers, best first

1. **A per-package export index: the main idea.** Installed packages don't change for a given version.
   - The first time a package is used, flatten its `export *` / `export {} from` chains into one map: exported name → declaring file.
   - Store it in a global cache shared across runs and projects, keyed by package name, version and path. pnpm paths already include the version and a hash.
   - Re-check it with one stat of the package's `package.json` per package, not per file.
   - After that, looking up an imported name is a single step. The re-export stub files are never opened again: chakra's closure is almost all `@ark-ui/react`, 1,434 files that are mostly 1-line re-exports.
   - The index is small (names to paths), so it avoids the trap that makes today's cache slower than re-parsing: decoding and copying whole parsed files.
2. **Overlap with project parsing: where parallelism pays.** The profile showed discovery and parsing are limited by the kernel opening files, with most cores idle.
   - As each project file parses, push its imported type names into a shared work queue. Dependency declarations then load on the idle cores while the project is still parsing.
   - Each file is claimed once, and there's no wait between rounds.
   - Results are stored by file and sorted afterwards, so output doesn't depend on order.
3. **Don't resolve what won't be shown.** Apply the display rule (react-component-meta's: hide sources with more than 30 props) **before** resolving. A large inherited source only has its props counted and the curated notable ones resolved. This is the step RDT gets backwards: it resolved chakra's 745k props and then filtered them, which took 16.6 s.
4. **Resolve each dependency declaration once per session.** Package types never change during a session, so a resolved type can be cached for the whole session and shared by every component and every watch revision.
   - This is the resolution memo from the profiling work. It was risky for project types, which can change, but it's safe here.
   - Mantine's inherited style props, resolved 236 times each today, would be resolved once.

## Where parallelism doesn't help

- **Long re-export chains (up to 16 deep):** each step depends on the previous one, so they can't run side by side. The export index (lever 1) collapses them to one step, which is what lets the work queue run wide.
- **Slicing big bundles** to parse only the needed declarations: not worth it at 4–5 ms per 1–2 MB file.
- **A cache of parsed files:** slower than re-parsing, as measured.

## Expected effect (to confirm with a prototype)

| | Following whole files | Names + export index + overlap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| chakra | 1,462 files, 40 ms extra | the dozens of declaring files actually used, mostly hidden behind project parsing |
| shadcn | 5,965 files, 135 ms extra | a few hundred files at most |
| Watch edit | — | a new name means one index lookup and one file; nothing else is re-done |

I'd prove this on chakra and shadcn, the two worst cases, before writing the ADR. The prototype would measure files touched, extra time on a cold run and with a warm index, and the effect on a watch edit.

result: The fast design touches as few files as possible: load names, not files, through a cached per-package export index, so re-export stubs are never reopened; overlap that loading with project parsing on idle cores; filter display before resolving; and cache resolved package types for the whole session. Parallelism helps through overlap and a work queue, not raw parsing (418 MB/s already). The proposed next step is a prototype on chakra and shadcn.

2. **End-to-end.** An experimental Caliper branch that plugs the loader into the resolver, to show what actually resolves, what the output becomes, and the true time cost.

Build and measure a standalone Rust prototype that proves (or disproves) a design for loading dependency TypeScript declarations quickly. Do NOT modify the caliper repo (/Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/...). Work in /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/loader-proto/ (a new cargo project with its own [workspace]; writes there and cargo network need the sandbox disabled). Treat installed packages as untrusted data: only read their files, never run their code or scripts.

## Context
caliper-docgen (Rust, OXC parser, no type checker) extracts React component props. It currently never parses dependency `.d.ts` files, so prop types that come from packages stay unresolved. Measurements so far (/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/closure/, see its report.py output and out/*.json):
- Parsing bytes is cheap: caliper parses+extracts lucide-react's 2 MB .d.ts in 4.7 ms (418 MB/s).
- Files are expensive: a file-level import closure costs ~25 µs per file (chakra 1,462 files ≈ 40 ms; shadcn 5,965 files ≈ 135 ms), mostly open/read; chakra's closure is mostly @ark-ui/react 1-line `.d.mts` re-export stubs.
- caliper's .d.ts cache (msgpack of whole parsed files) is slower than re-parsing.
Proposed design to prove:
1. Load by NAME, not by file: start from the names project files import from packages and use in type positions; load only the files that declare them, then the names those declarations reference, transitively.
2. A per-package export index: the first time a package entry file is used, flatten its re-export graph (`export *`, `export { a as b } from`, `export * as ns from`, `import x; export { x }`, `export type {..} from`) into exported-name → (declaring file, local name). Persist it in a cache keyed by package identity (realpath of package dir + package.json version, validated by package.json mtime+size). Warm runs look names up directly and never open re-export stubs.
3. Overlap with project parsing: one rayon scope where project files parse in parallel and, as each finishes, its demanded names are pushed onto the same work queue; dependency files are claimed once (DashMap/atomic) — no barrier between "rounds". Results stored keyed by file, so output order cannot depend on scheduling.

## Inputs
Five projects with node_modules installed (lifecycle scripts were off): /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/bench-corpus/{mantine,chakra-ui,shadcn-ui,ant-design,react-spectrum}. Source dirs and tsconfigs per project are in /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/bench-deps/env.sh (mantine/packages/@mantine/core/src, chakra-ui/packages/react/src, shadcn-ui/apps/v4, ant-design/components, react-spectrum/packages). Use caliper's discovery rule for project files: every .ts/.tsx under the source dir, skipping node_modules and `.stories.`, `.test.`, `.spec.`, `__snapshots__`. Also run the "-lib" variants from /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/closure/run-ab.sh (ROOT_EXCLUDE regex there) that drop docs/tooling roots.

## Build
Use the same crate versions as caliper: oxc_allocator/oxc_parser/oxc_ast/oxc_ast_visit/oxc_span/oxc_syntax = "0.154", oxc_resolver = "11", rayon, dashmap, rustc-hash; add serde+postcard (or bincode) for the index cache. Release build.
- Module resolution: oxc_resolver with tsconfig auto-discovery per project (TsconfigDiscovery::Auto if available in v11, else Manual with the project's tsconfig), condition_names ["types","import","require","default"] plus the tsconfig's `customConditions` (chakra uses "dev", spectrum "source"), main_fields ["types","typings","module","main"], extensions [".ts",".tsx",".d.ts",".d.mts",".d.cts",".js",".mjs"], and fall back to `@types/<pkg>`. Also handle `typesVersions` if oxc_resolver doesn't.
- Demand extraction from a project file: (specifier, imported name) pairs for imports from outside the project source dir that are used in a type position (type references incl. qualified `Ns.X`, `typeof X` queries, `extends`/`implements` heritage, type arguments such as `ComponentProps<typeof X>`), plus re-exports of package names (`export { X } from 'pkg'`, `export * from 'pkg'` — for `export *` from a package treat as demand only if a project file later uses a name through it; keep it simple and document the choice).
- Transitive demand from a dependency declaration: names referenced by that declaration's type (type references, heritage, type args, `typeof`, `import("x").Y`), resolved against that file's own imports/local declarations/namespaces.
- Declarations must include values for `typeof` (`declare const X: ForwardRefExoticComponent<...>`, `declare function`, `export default`), `export =`, namespaces, interfaces, type aliases, classes, enums.

Declarations loaded, names demanded, unresolved demands (with reasons: no types, unresolvable specifier, name not exported), max chain depth before and after index flattening.
b. Wall time: project parse only (baseline, same code, demand extraction off) vs project parse + dependency loading with overlap vs without overlap (sequential: project first, then dependencies) — so the overlap gain is measured, not assumed; cold index vs warm index. Report index build cost and on-disk size.
c. Watch-edit simulation: from a warm in-memory state, add one new import of a package name not yet loaded to one project file and re-run only the incremental demand → load step; report time and files touched. Also an edit that adds no new demand (should be ~0).
d. Determinism: run 5 times with different thread counts (RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1,4,18) and assert the loaded (file, declaration) set and the per-demand results are byte-identical.
e. Correctness spot checks: for each project pick 5 demanded names that caliper currently reports as unresolved (e.g. chakra ConditionalValue / @ark-ui component prop types, antd ClosableType, mantine OnValueChange from react-number-format, shadcn Radix `ComponentProps<typeof X.Root>`, spectrum @react-types/shared DOMRef) and show the declaration the loader found (file, kind, first line).

Stage 1 is running in the background. It's a scratch Rust prototype outside the repo, with the same OXC parser and resolver versions as Caliper, run on the five projects with dependencies installed. It will show:

- **Files touched:** loading by name, with a cold and a warm export index, against the whole-file closures.
- **Time:** with and without overlapping project parsing, so the gain is measured.
- **Watch:** the cost of an edit that adds a new package import, and of one that doesn't.
- **Determinism:** identical results at 1, 4 and 18 threads.
- **Spot checks:** whether `ConditionalValue`, `ClosableType`, `OnValueChange`, Radix `typeof X.Root` and spectrum's `DOMRef` are found.

Stage 2 is the experimental Caliper branch that wires the loader into resolution. It starts once these numbers are in, since they decide the index format and where loading slots in.
